summary: Defines a generic template for signed objects in the RPKI, which use the Cryptographic Message Syntax as the wrapper. Other RPKI object types, like ROAs and manifests, follow this template. It was later updated by RFC 9589.

eli5.summary: Many RPKI documents need a signature in the same way. This is the shared envelope they all use, with the same place to put the signature.

questions: what is an rpki signed object
what does cms have to do with rpki
subtitle: The common CMS envelope that every signed object in the RPKI is built from.

tldr.problem: The RPKI carries assertions about IP address and AS number resources in signed objects that are not X.509 certificates, and each type of object needs the same signing wrapper.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6488 profiles the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) signed-data object, DER encoded, with one embedded end-entity certificate and one signer, and sets validation steps all signed objects share.
tldr.outcome: Each new object type, such as the ROA and the manifest, only has to define its own OID, payload syntax and extra validation. The RFC is updated by RFC 9589.

today: RFC 6488 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it is updated by RFC 9589.

sections.title: Why a Signed Object Template
sections.content:
The Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI) supports assertions by current resource holders of IP (v4 and v6) address space and AS numbers. Resource information is carried in X.509 certificates, while other assertions are expressed as digitally signed, non-X.509 data structures called signed objects.

RFC 6488 standardizes a template for these objects, using the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) as the encapsulation format. CMS was chosen to take advantage of existing open source software. The template is not a full specification of any object: it holds only what is common to all of them. RFC 6482 is cited as an example, specifying the Route Origination Authorization (ROA).
sections.eli5: Imagine every official letter in a club uses the same kind of signed envelope. This RFC describes that envelope, not the letters.

sections.title: The Signed-Data Profile
sections.content:
An RPKI signed object is a profile of the CMS signed-data object and MUST be encoded using the ASN.1 Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER). The outer content type is id-signedData, OID 1.2.840.113549.1.7.2.

The profile fixes several choices. The version MUST be 3. digestAlgorithms MUST contain exactly one digest algorithm OID, taken from RFC 6485. certificates MUST be present and hold exactly one certificate, the end-entity (EE) certificate needed to validate the object. crls MUST be omitted. The SignerInfos set MUST contain only a single SignerInfo.

The eContentType and eContent are left undefined here and MUST be specified by the Standards Track document defining each object. Because the profile has no version numbers, each object type is RECOMMENDED to include a version number in its eContent.
sections.eli5: The envelope has strict rules: one signer, one ID card for that signer, and no extras. Only what is inside the envelope changes between document types.

sections.title: The SignerInfo and Signed Attributes
sections.content:
In the SignerInfo, the version MUST be 3, matching the choice of SubjectKeyIdentifier for the sid, which MUST be the SubjectKeyIdentifier of the EE certificate carried in the object. The digest and signature algorithms MUST conform to RFC 6485. unsignedAttrs MUST be omitted.

The signedAttrs element MUST be present and MUST include the content-type attribute (OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.3), which has to match the eContentType, and the message-digest attribute (OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.4). The signer MAY also include the signing-time attribute (OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.5), the binary-signing-time attribute (OID 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.2.46), or both. No other signed attributes are allowed.

Each attribute may appear only once, with a single value. Presence or absence of the two time attributes MUST NOT affect validity.
sections.eli5: The signature covers a small label that says what kind of document it is and a fingerprint of its contents. Optional time stamps may be added, but nothing else.

sections.title: Validating a Signed Object
sections.content:
A relying party MUST validate a signed object before using it. The checks may be done in any order. First, the syntax must comply with the profile, covering items such as: content type is SignedData, versions are 3, exactly one EE certificate whose SubjectKeyIdentifier matches the sid, no crls, required attributes present and no disallowed ones, no unsignedAttrs, algorithms conform to RFC 6485, and DER encoding.

Second, the EE certificate's public key must verify the signature. Third, the EE certificate must be valid in the RPKI per RFC 6487, which includes a valid certification path from a trust anchor.

An invalid object MUST be discarded and treated as though no signed object were present. These checks are necessary but not sufficient: further validation specific to the object type MUST also be done. An object stops being valid when its EE certificate expires or is revoked.
sections.eli5: Before trusting a letter, you check the envelope follows the rules, the signature matches, and the signer's ID is real. If any check fails, you act as if the letter never arrived.

sections.title: Defining a New Signed Object
sections.content:
Each RPKI signed object MUST be defined in an Internet Standards Track document based on this profile. That document supplies three things: a single OID used for both the eContentType and the content-type attribute, the syntax of the eContent payload, and any additional validation steps that a relying party must perform on top of the generic ones.

IANA created a registry of RPKI Signed Objects, managed by IETF Standards Action, with the name, the eContentType OID and the specification. It started with two entries: ROA (1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.24, RFC 6482) and Manifest (1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.26, RFC 6486).
sections.eli5: To make a new kind of signed document, you just say what it is called, what goes inside, and any extra checks. The envelope is already done.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: There is no assumption of confidentiality for data in an RPKI signed object. Integrity and authenticity rest on verifying the object's digital signature and validating the EE certificate used for that verification. Signed objects are expected to be stored in publicly accessible repositories. Because CMS is the encapsulation format, the security considerations of CMS (RFC 5652) apply too.
sections.eli5: These documents are public on purpose. The signature is there to prove they are real and unchanged, not to keep them secret.
